Graphs attaining an upper bound on the mixed metric dimension

Shi Chen and Xuanlong Ma Note: Corresponding author Affiliation: School of Science, Xi’an Petroleum University, Xi’an 710065, P. R. China
Abstract

Given a graph GG, we show that the mixed metric dimension of GG is exactly ℓ⁡(G)+2​c​(G)\ell(G)+2c(G) if and only if GG is either a cactus graph in which every cycle has precisely one vertex of degree at least 33, or a balanced Θ\Theta-graph, where ℓ⁡(G)\ell(G) and c⁡(G)c(G) denote the number of leaves and the cyclomatic number of GG, respectively. This provides an affirmative answer to a conjecture proposed by Sedlar and Škrekovski (2021).

Key words: Mixed metric dimension; Cyclomatic number; Cactus graph; Θ\Theta-graph

2010 MSC: 05C25; 05C12

†† E-mail addresses: nuoyoushi@gmail.com (Chen), xuanlma@xsyu.edu.cn (Ma)

1 Introduction

All graphs considered in this paper are finite, simple, and connected. We always use GG to denote a graph. Denote by V⁡(G)V(G) and E⁡(G)E(G) the vertex set and edge set of GG, respectively. The minimum degree of a graph GG, denoted by δ⁡(G)\delta(G), is the smallest integer kk such that there exists a vertex with degree kk in this graph. For two vertices uu and vv of a graph GG, the distance between uu and vv is denoted by dG​(u,v){\rm d}_{G}(u,v), or simply by d⁡(u,v){\rm d}(u,v) when no confusion can arise. For distinct x,y∈V⁡(G)x,y\in V(G), we say a vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) distinguishes xx and yy whenever d⁡(v,x)≠d⁡(v,y).{\rm d}(v,x)\neq{\rm d}(v,y). A subset S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is called a metric generator of GG if for every pair of distinct vertices x,y∈V⁡(G)x,y\in V(G), there exists a vertex in SS such that this vertex distinguishes xx and yy. A metric generator of GG with minimum cardinality is called a metric basis of GG, and the cardinality of a metric basis is referred to as the metric dimension of GG.

In the 1970s, the concept of metric dimension was introduced independently by Harary and Melter [3], and Slater [10]. Their aim is to distinguish vertices of a graph using distances. The metric dimension of a graph has a wide range of applications, including robot navigation in networks, chemistry, pattern recognition, and image processing, and so on. See the survey [11] for more results and applications of the metric dimension. In 2018, as a further variation of the classical notion of a metric generator, Kelenc et al. [7] introduced the concept of an edge metric generator, which is to distinguish the edges of a graph by means of distances from a prescribed set of vertices. For a vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) and an edge e={u,w}∈E⁡(G)e=\{u,w\}\in E(G), the distance between vv and ee is defined by

d⁡(v,e)=min⁡{d⁡(v,u),d⁡(v,w)}.{\rm d}(v,e)=\min\{{\rm d}(v,u),{\rm d}(v,w)\}.

A vertex x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) is said to distinguish two distinct edges e1,e2∈E⁡(G)e_{1},e_{2}\in E(G) if d⁡(x,e1)≠d⁡(x,e2).{\rm d}(x,e_{1})\neq{\rm d}(x,e_{2}). A set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is called an edge metric generator for GG provided that every pair of distinct edges of GG is distinguished by some vertex in SS. An edge metric generator of minimum cardinality is called an edge metric basis of GG, and its cardinality is called the edge metric dimension of GG.

For a graph GG, let

O⁡(G)=V⁡(G)∪E⁡(G).O(G)=V(G)\cup E(G).

We say a vertex vv of (G)(G) distinguishes two distinct elements x,y∈O⁡(G)x,y\in O(G) (vertices or edges) if d⁡(v,x)≠d⁡(v,y).{\rm d}(v,x)\neq{\rm d}(v,y). For a subset SS of V⁡(G)V(G), we say SS is a mixed metric generator of GG provided that, for every pair of distinct elements x,y∈O⁡(G)x,y\in O(G), there exists a vertex in SS such that this vertex distinguishes xx and yy. The cardinality of a mixed metric generator with minimum size, denoted by dimm​(G){\rm dim_{m}}(G), is called the mixed metric dimension of GG. Kelenc et al. [6] first introduced the concept of a mixed metric dimension.

In [6], the authors determined the mixed metric dimension of several families of graphs and established an upper bound in terms of the girth. They also proved that computing the mixed metric dimension of a general graph is NP-hard. A leaf of GG is a vertex of degree 11. Denote by ℓ⁡(G)\ell(G) the number of all leaves of GG. The cyclomatic number of GG, denoted by c⁡(G)c(G), is the number of independent cycles of GG. It is well known that c⁡(G)=|E⁡(G)|−|V⁡(G)|+1c(G)=|E(G)|-|V(G)|+1. In [9], Sedlar and Škrekovski obtained the exact value of the mixed metric dimension of a unicyclic graph and they proposed the following conjecture:

Conjecture 1.1

([9, Conjecture 13]) Let GG be a connected graph which is not a cycle. Then dimm​(G)≤ℓ⁡(G)+2​c​(G){\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq\ell(G)+2c(G).

In [9], the authors showed that Conjecture 1.1 holds for trees and 33-connected graphs. A Theta graph (or Θ\Theta-graph) is a graph with exactly two vertices of degree 33 and all others of degree 22. Let HH be a Θ\Theta-graph with distinct vertices u,vu,v of degree 33. Then HH is called balanced provided that the lengths of all three paths connecting uu and vv differ by at most 11; Otherwise, HH is called unbalanced. In [8], the authors proved that Conjecture 1.1 holds for all Θ\Theta-graph. In 2025, Chakraborty et al. [1] proved that Conjecture 1.1 is valid for a connected graph which is not a tree such that ℓ⁡(G)≥1\ell(G)\geq 1, and a connected graph GG with ℓ⁡(G)=0\ell(G)=0 and has a cut-vertex. In [4], the authors gave some graphs satisfying Conjecture 1.1. Recently, Chen and Ma [2] showed that for a 22-connected graph GG which is not a cycle, the mixed metric dimension of GG is at most 2​c​(G)2c(G). As an immediate application, Conjecture 1.1 was proved.

If GG is a cycle, then by [6, Theorem 3.8 and Proposition 4.1] we have dimm​(G)=3{\rm dim_{m}}(G)=3. As a result, dimm​(G)=ℓ⁡(G)+2​c​(G){\rm dim_{m}}(G)=\ell(G)+2c(G) is not valid for a cycle. Moreover, by [8, Corollary 8], dimm​(G)=ℓ⁡(G)+2​c​(G){\rm dim_{m}}(G)=\ell(G)+2c(G) is valid for a balanced Θ\Theta-graph GG. In the concluding section of [8], the authors proposed the following conjecture:

Conjecture 1.2

([8, Conjecture 12]) Let GG be a graph. Then

dimm​(G)=ℓ⁡(G)+2​c​(G){\rm dim_{m}}(G)=\ell(G)+2c(G) (1)

if and only if GG is either a cactus graph in which every cycle has precisely one vertex of degree at least 33 or a balanced Θ\Theta-graph.

This paper will provide an affirmative answer to Conjecture 1.2.

2 Preliminaries

In order to prove Conjecture 1.2, we will establish several lemmas in this section.

Lemma 2.1

Let GG be a 22-connected graph with c⁡(G)=2c(G)=2. Then GG is a Θ\Theta-graph.

Proof. Note that GG is not a cycle and δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2. Then we have

∑v∈V⁡(G)(deg⁡(v)−2)=2|E⁡(G)|−2​|V⁡(G)|=2​c​(G)−2=2.\sum_{v\in V(G)}(\deg(v)-2)=2|E(G)|-2|V(G)|=2c(G)-2=2.

We conclude that the degree of a vertex of GG is at most 44.

Suppose, for a contradiction, that GG has a vertex uu with degree 44. Then all other vertices of GG have degree 22. Let x,y,z,wx,y,z,w be the four vertices adjacent to uu. If we delete uu in GG, then any of x,y,z,wx,y,z,w has degree 11. It follows that the subgraph of GG obtained by delete uu is the union of two disjoint paths. Thus, uu is a cut-vertex of GG, this contradicts that GG is 22-connected.

Thus, GG has precisely two vertices with degree 33, and all other vertices have degree 22. This means that GG is a Θ\Theta-graph, as desired. □\hfill\Box\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt

Denote by L⁡(G)L(G) the set of all leaves of GG. A block of a graph is a maximal connected subgraph that has no cut-vertex. Given a connected graph GG with at least a cut-vertex, we next define the graph B⁡(G)B(G) with vertex set ℬ∪C\mathcal{B}\cup C, where ℬ\mathcal{B} is the set of all blocks of GG, and CC is the set of all cut-vertices of GG. In fact, B⁡(G)B(G) is bipartite with bipartition (ℬ,C)(\mathcal{B},C), and a block B∈ℬB\in\mathcal{B} and a cut-vertex v∈Cv\in C is adjacent if and only if v∈V⁡(B)v\in V(B). Clearly, B⁡(G)B(G) is a tree, and so we call B⁡(G)B(G) the block tree of GG (cf. [5]).

For a connected graph GG with at least a cut-vertex, let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the set of all blocks containing a cycle. For D∈ℱD\in\mathcal{F}, let XDX_{D} be a mixed metric generator of DD, and let CDC_{D} be the set of the cut-vertices in DD.

Lemma 2.3

Let GG be a connected graph with at least a cut-vertex. Then

L⁡(G)∪(⋃D∈ℱXD∖CD)L(G)\cup(\bigcup_{D\in\mathcal{F}}X_{D}\setminus C_{D})

is a mixed metric generator of GG.

Proof. If every B∈ℬB\in\mathcal{B} has no cycle, then GG is a tree, and so L⁡(G)L(G) is a mixed metric generator of GG, as desired. In the following, assume that ℱ≠∅\mathcal{F}\neq\emptyset and let D∈ℱD\in\mathcal{F}. Now let cc be a cut-vertex belonging to DD, and let E∈ℬ∖{D}E\in\mathcal{B}\setminus\{D\} with c∈Ec\in E.

Claim A. Suppose that EE belongs to ℱ\mathcal{F}. Then (XD∪XE)∖{c}(X_{D}\cup X_{E})\setminus\{c\} is a mixed metric generator of D∪ED\cup E.

If two distinct elements of O⁡(D)O(D) (resp. O⁡(E)O(E)) are distinguished by cc, then they must be distinguished by an element of XE∖{c}X_{E}\setminus\{c\} (resp. XD∖{c}X_{D}\setminus\{c\}). Now take z1∈O⁡(D)∖{c},z2∈O⁡(E)∖{c}.z_{1}\in O(D)\setminus\{c\},z_{2}\in O(E)\setminus\{c\}. Without loss of generality, let dD∪E​(z1,c)≤dD∪E​(z2,c){\rm d}_{D\cup E}(z_{1},c)\leq{\rm d}_{D\cup E}(z_{2},c).

Suppose, for a contradiction, that for any x∈XD∖{c}x\in X_{D}\setminus\{c\}, we have that

dD​(x,z1)=dD​(x,c)+dD​(c,z1).{\rm d}_{D}(x,z_{1})={\rm d}_{D}(x,c)+{\rm d}_{D}(c,z_{1}). (6)

If d⁡(c,z1)=0{\rm d}(c,z_{1})=0, then z1z_{1} is an edge with an endpoint cc, which implies that cc and z1z_{1} cannot be distinguished by any of XD∪{c}X_{D}\cup\{c\} by (6), a contradiction. Now let dD​(c,z1)=r>0{\rm d}_{D}(c,z_{1})=r>0. Choose a shortest path form cc to vrv_{r} in DD as follows:

(c,v1,v2,…,vr−1,vr),(c,v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{r-1},v_{r}),

where if z1z_{1} is a vertex, then vr=z1v_{r}=z_{1}; otherwise, vrv_{r} is an endpoint of z1z_{1}. Then

dD​(x,vr−1)=dD​(x,c)+r−1=dD​(x,c)+dD​(c,{vr−1,vr})=dD​(x,{vr−1,vr}){\rm d}_{D}(x,v_{r-1})={\rm d}_{D}(x,c)+r-1={\rm d}_{D}(x,c)+{\rm d}_{D}(c,\{v_{r-1},v_{r}\})={\rm d}_{D}(x,\{v_{r-1},v_{r}\}) (7)

and

dD​(c,vr−1)=dD​(c,{vr−1,vr}).{\rm d}_{D}(c,v_{r-1})={\rm d}_{D}(c,\{v_{r-1},v_{r}\}). (8)

Naturally, if vr−1=cv_{r-1}=c, then both (7) and (8) hold. It follows that, in this case, {vr−1,vr}\{v_{r-1},v_{r}\} and vr−1v_{r-1} cannot be distinguished by any of XD∪{c}X_{D}\cup\{c\} by (6), this contradicts that XDX_{D} is a mixed metric generator of DD.

We conclude that there exists y∈XD∖{c}y\in X_{D}\setminus\{c\}, such that dD​(y,z1)≤dD​(x,c)+dD​(c,z1).{\rm d}_{D}(y,z_{1})\leq{\rm d}_{D}(x,c)+{\rm d}_{D}(c,z_{1}). It follows that

dD∪E​(y,z1)<dD∪E​(y,c)+dD∪E​(c,z1)≤dD∪E​(y,c)+dD∪E​(c,z2)=dD∪E​(y,z2),{\rm d}_{D\cup E}(y,z_{1})<{\rm d}_{D\cup E}(y,c)+{\rm d}_{D\cup E}(c,z_{1})\leq{\rm d}_{D\cup E}(y,c)+{\rm d}_{D\cup E}(c,z_{2})={\rm d}_{D\cup E}(y,z_{2}),

which means that z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} are distinguished by yy. As a result, (XD∪XE)∖{c}(X_{D}\cup X_{E})\setminus\{c\} is a mixed metric generator of D∪ED\cup E, so Claim A holds.

Claim B. Suppose that EE is an edge {c,c′}\{c,c^{\prime}\} and c′c^{\prime} is a leaf. Then (XD∪{c′})∖{c}(X_{D}\cup\{c^{\prime}\})\setminus\{c\} is a mixed metric generator of D∪ED\cup E.

Claim B easily follows from the proof of Claim A.

Now, suppose that EE is a bridge, say {c,c1}\{c,c_{1}\}, where c1c_{1} is not a leaf. Then there exists E1∈ℬE_{1}\in\mathcal{B} such that c1∈V⁡(E1)c_{1}\in V(E_{1}). Certainly, E1E_{1} can also be a bridge, say {c1,c2}\{c_{1},c_{2}\}, where c2c_{2} is not a leaf. Now let every edge of this path P=(c,c1,c2,…,cn)P=(c,c_{1},c_{2},\ldots,c_{n}) is a bridge, and let En∈ℬE_{n}\in\mathcal{B} be either an edge {cn,c′}\{c_{n},c^{\prime}\} and c′c^{\prime} is a leaf, or a block containing cnc_{n} and belonging to ℱ\mathcal{F}. If En∈ℱE_{n}\in\mathcal{F}, then it is similar to Claim A, (XD∪XEn)∖{c,cn}(X_{D}\cup X_{E_{n}})\setminus\{c,c_{n}\} is a mixed metric generator of D∪E∪PD\cup E\cup P. If not, it is similar to Claim B, (XD∪{c′})∖{c}(X_{D}\cup\{c^{\prime}\})\setminus\{c\} is a mixed metric generator of D∪E∪PD\cup E\cup P.

Finally, by the block tree of GG, we can “glue” all the blocks of GG together at their cut vertices. As a result, L(G)∪(∪D∈ℱXD∖CD)L(G)\cup(\cup_{D\in\mathcal{F}}X_{D}\setminus C_{D}) is a mixed metric generator of GG, as desired. □\hfill\Box\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt

Given a graph GG, let

𝒮={v∈V⁡(G):deg⁡(v)≥3}.\mathcal{S}=\{v\in V(G):\deg(v)\geq 3\}.

A thread in a graph GG is a path whose internal vertices all have degree 22 in GG. Let P=(p0,p1,…,pl)P=(p_{0},p_{1},\ldots,p_{l}) be a thread of GG. We use G−P0G-P^{0} to denote the subgraph of GG that is obtained by removing the internal vertices of this thread PP and keeping the endpoints p0p_{0} and plp_{l}. If G−P0G-P^{0} is connected and l<dG−P0​(p0,pl)l<{\rm d}_{G-P^{0}}(p_{0},p_{l}), then PP is called a short thread of GG. If deg⁡(p0)≥3\deg(p_{0})\geq 3 and deg⁡(pl)≥3\deg(p_{l})\geq 3, then this thread PP is called maximal.

Lemma 2.4

Let GG be 22-connected with c⁡(G)≥3c(G)\geq 3. Then dimm​(G)≤2​c​(G)−1{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq 2c(G)-1.

Proof. Let c⁡(G)=nc(G)=n. If every thread of GG is short, it follows from [2, Lemmas 2.3 and 2.5] that dimm​(G)≤|𝒮|≤2​n−2<2​n−1{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq|\mathcal{S}|\leq 2n-2<2n-1, as desired. In the following, we always assume that GG has a maximal thread P=(u=p0,p1,…,pl=v)P=(u=p_{0},p_{1},\ldots,p_{l}=v) such that l≥dH​(u,v)l\geq{\rm d}_{H}(u,v), where H=G−P0H=G-P^{0}. Then clearly, HH is connected and has no leaves. Thus, we have that

c⁡(H)=|E⁡(H)|−|V⁡(H)|+1=(|E⁡(G)|−l)−(|V⁡(G)|−(l−1))+1,c(H)=|E(H)|-|V(H)|+1=(|E(G)|-l)-(|V(G)|-(l-1))+1,

namely,

n=c⁡(G)=c⁡(H)+1.n=c(G)=c(H)+1. (9)

To end our proof, we now proceed by induction on nn.

Suppose first that n=3n=3. Then c⁡(H)=2c(H)=2 by (9). Assume that HH is a 22-connected graph. Then Lemma 2.1 implies that HH is a Θ\Theta-graph. If HH is an unbalanced Θ\Theta-graph, then in view of [8, Theorem 10], we obtain that dimm​(H)=3{\rm dim_{m}}(H)=3, which implies that dimm​(G)≤dimm​(H)+2≤2​n−1{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq{\rm dim_{m}}(H)+2\leq 2n-1 by [2, Lemma 2.4], as required. Next, assume that HH is a balanced Θ\Theta-graph. Then, it follows from Lemma 2.2 that there exists a mixed metric generator ℛ\mathcal{R} of HH such that

|ℛ|=4,u∈ℛ,dH​(r,u)≥dH​(r,v)​ for some r∈ℛ.|\mathcal{R}|=4,~~u\in\mathcal{R},~~{\rm d}_{H}(r,u)\geq{\rm d}_{H}(r,v)\text{ for some $r\in\mathcal{R}$}.

Note that dimm​(H)=4{\rm dim_{m}}(H)=4 by [8, Theorem 7]. Thus, ℛ\mathcal{R} is a mixed metric generator of HH with the smallest cardinality. Now let w=p⌈l/2⌉w=p_{\lceil l/2\rceil}. In view of [2, Lemma 2.4], it is obvious that ℛ∪{u,w}=ℛ∪{w}\mathcal{R}\cup\{u,w\}=\mathcal{R}\cup\{w\} is a mixed metric generator of GG. It follows that dimm​(G)≤2​n−1{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq 2n-1, as desired.

Assume that HH is not 22-connected. Note that HH has no leaves and contains at least a cut-vertex. It follows from c⁡(H)=2c(H)=2 that HH is a cactus graph with exactly two cycles. Now let CuC_{u} and CvC_{v} be two distinct cycles with u∈Cuu\in C_{u} and v∈Cvv\in C_{v}, and let aua_{u} and ava_{v} be cut-vertices with au∈Cua_{u}\in C_{u} and av∈Cva_{v}\in C_{v}. Clearly, u≠auu\neq a_{u} and v≠avv\neq a_{v}, but aua_{u} and ava_{v} are not necessarily distinct. For CuC_{u}, taking a thread from uu to aua_{u} satisfying the hypotheses of [2, Lemma 2.4], we deduce that there exists x∈V⁡(Cu)∖{u,au}x\in V(C_{u})\setminus\{u,a_{u}\} such that {u,au,x}\{u,a_{u},x\} is a mixed metric generator of CuC_{u}. Similarly, we may assume that {v,av,y}\{v,a_{v},y\} is a mixed metric generator of CvC_{v}. It follows from Lemma 2.3 that {u,v,x,y}\{u,v,x,y\} is a mixed metric generator of HH. Write, now, w=p⌈l/2⌉w=p_{\lceil l/2\rceil}. By [2, Lemma 2.4] again, we conclude that {u,v,x,y}∪{w}\{u,v,x,y\}\cup\{w\} is a mixed metric generator of GG. As a consequence, dimm​(G)≤2​n−1{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq 2n-1, as desired.

Now, assume that the statement holds for every 22-connected graph whose cyclomatic number is at least 44 and less than nn. We then prove this result holds for nn.

Case 1. HH is 22-connected.

If c⁡(H)=2c(H)=2, then c⁡(G)=3c(G)=3 by (9), which implies that the required result holds by the above proof. Suppose nest that c⁡(H)≥3c(H)\geq 3. Note that c⁡(H)<nc(H)<n. Then by the induction hypothesis, we deduce that dimm​(H)≤2​c​(H)−1{\rm dim_{m}}(H)\leq 2c(H)-1. It follows from [2, Lemma 2.4] that dimm​(G)≤dimm​(H)+2{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq{\rm dim_{m}}(H)+2, which implies that

dimm​(G)≤dimm​(H)+2≤2​c​(H)−1+2=2​c​(H)+1=2​n−1{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq{\rm dim_{m}}(H)+2\leq 2c(H)-1+2=2c(H)+1=2n-1

by (9), as desired.

Case 2. HH is not 22-connected.

Then HH has at least a cut-vertex. As a result, HH has at least two blocks containing a cycle. Let DD be a block of HH that contains a cycle. If DD is a cycle, then [9, Lemma 4] implies that we can find a mixed metric generator XDX_{D} containing a cut-vertex. Suppose that c⁡(D)=2c(D)=2. Then DD is a Θ\Theta-graph by Lemma 2.1. If DD is unbalanced, then [8, Theorem 10] manes that dimm​(D)=2​c​(D)−1{\rm dim_{m}}(D)=2c(D)-1; Otherwise, by Lemma 2.2 we may choose a mixed metric generator XDX_{D} containing a cut-vertex. If c⁡(D)≥3c(D)\geq 3, since DD is 22-connected and c⁡(D)<nc(D)<n, we have dimm​(D)≤2​c​(D)−1{\rm dim_{m}}(D)\leq 2c(D)-1 by the induction hypothesis, which implies that we can take a mixed metric generator XDX_{D} of DD that has size 2​c​(D)−12c(D)-1.

Case 2.1. HH has a block D′D^{\prime} that contains a cycle but is not itself a cycle.

In view of Lemma 2.3, we have that

dimm​(H)\displaystyle{\rm dim_{m}}(H) ≤|⋃D∈ℱ(XD∖CD)|\displaystyle\leq\Big|\bigcup_{D\in\mathcal{F}}(X_{D}\setminus C_{D})\Big| (10)
≤|⋃D∈ℱ∖{D′}(XD∖CD)|+|XD′∖CD′|\displaystyle\leq\Big|\bigcup_{D\in\mathcal{F}\setminus\{D^{\prime}\}}(X_{D}\setminus C_{D})\Big|+\big|X_{D^{\prime}}\setminus C_{D^{\prime}}\big|
≤∑D∈ℱ∖{D′}2​c​(D)+2​c​(D′)−1\displaystyle\leq\sum_{D\in\mathcal{F}\setminus\{D^{\prime}\}}2c(D)+2c(D^{\prime})-1
=2​c​(H)−1.\displaystyle=2c(H)-1.

Now, from [2, Lemma 2.4], it follows that

dimm​(G)≤dimm​(H)+2≤2​c​(H)+1=2​c​(G)−1,{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq{\rm dim_{m}}(H)+2\leq 2c(H)+1=2c(G)-1,

as desired.

Case 2.2. Every D∈ℱD\in\mathcal{F} is a cycle.

In this case we have that HH is a cactus graph. By [9, Corollary 10], we conclude that dimm​(H)≤2​c​(H){\rm dim_{m}}(H)\leq 2c(H) and the equality is attained if and only if every cycle in HH has exactly one root vertex. If dimm​(H)≤2​c​(H)−1{\rm dim_{m}}(H)\leq 2c(H)-1, then the desired result follows from [2, Lemma 2.4]. Suppose now that dimm​(H)=2​c​(H){\rm dim_{m}}(H)=2c(H). Since GG is 22-connected, we deduce that HH is a cactus graph with exactly two cycles. As a result, we have that c⁡(H)=2c(H)=2, which implies that c⁡(G)=3c(G)=3, and the required result follows. □\hfill\Box\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt

3 An affirmative answer to Conjecture 1.2

We are now ready to prove Conjecture 1.2.

Proof of Conjecture 1.2. By [8, Corollary 8], (1) holds for a balanced Θ\Theta-graph GG. Moreover, it follows from [9, Theorem 9] that (1) holds for a cactus graph in which every cycle has precisely one vertex of degree at least 33. Thus, the sufficiency follows.

We next prove the necessity. Suppose that (1) holds for graph GG. If c⁡(G)=0c(G)=0, then GG is a tree, which implies that GG is a cactus graph in which every cycle has precisely one vertex of degree at least 33 (note that a tree has no cycles), as desired. In the following, we always assume that c⁡(G)≥1c(G)\geq 1.

Case 1. GG has no cut-vertices.

If c⁡(G)=1c(G)=1, then GG is a cycle, which implies that (1) is not valid by [6, Theorem 3.8 and Proposition 4.1]. Suppose that c⁡(G)=2c(G)=2. Then by Lemma 2.1, GG is a Θ\Theta-graph. Furthermore, if GG is an unbalanced Θ\Theta-graph, then by [8, Theorem 10] we have dimm​(G)=3{\rm dim_{m}}(G)=3, which implies (1) does not hold. Otherwise, GG is a balanced Θ\Theta-graph, as desired.

Now, suppose that c⁡(G)>2c(G)>2. Then Lemma 2.4 means that

dimm​(G)≤2​c​(G)−1<2​c​(G)≤ℓ⁡(G)+2​c​(G),{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq 2c(G)-1<2c(G)\leq\ell(G)+2c(G),

which is impossible.

Case 2. GG has at least a cut-vertex.

If GG has a block that contains a cycle but is not itself a cycle, then by Lemma 2.3, it is similar to (10), we deduce that dimm​(G)≤2​c​(G)−1{\rm dim_{m}}(G)\leq 2c(G)-1, which is impossible. It follows that every block of GG that contains a cycle is itself a cycle. As a result, GG is a cactus graph. Moreover, by [9, Theorem 9], we see that GG is a cactus graph in which every cycle has precisely one vertex of degree at least 33, as desired. □\hfill\Box\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt
